sections.overview: The common cockle is a burrowing marine bivalve native to European and north-west African coasts, especially sheltered tidal flats, estuaries and bays.
sections.identification: Its rounded, convex shell has strong radial ribs; it is commonly 1.5–3.5 cm long and resembles the lagoon cockle (C. glaucum), whose internal rib grooves extend farther across the shell.
sections.habitat: It lives just below the surface of sand or mud on the intertidal shore, using a muscular foot to burrow and resist wave-driven water movement.
sections.diet: It is a suspension feeder: water drawn through an inhalant siphon brings phytoplankton and suspended organic matter to its gills.
sections.behavior: The cockle remains buried with its short siphons near the sediment surface, where it can feed while largely protected within the sediment.
sections.reproduction: It has separate sexes and releases eggs and sperm into the water; spawning generally occurs from spring through summer, after which planktonic larvae settle and begin a buried life.
sections.ecology: The related C. glaucum is often found in lagoons and brackish water and can be confused with it; cockle beds also provide food for fish, crabs and shorebirds, including the plovers described in this bestiary.
sections.conservation: It is locally harvested and its abundance fluctuates with recruitment, weather and predation; studies in the Wadden Sea show why stock condition matters to both shellfish fisheries and birds that eat cockles.
